7 How much of the ecosystem inherits the pattern

Table 2 covers thirteen tokenizers that we selected, which is precisely the kind of evidence a reader should discount. To replace selection with a rule, we classified the pre-tokenizer of every model in two listings from the HuggingFace Hub (Wolf et al., 2020): the top 2,000 repositories by 30day downloads, and the top 2,000 carrying the text-generation pipeline tag, 3,479 distinct repositories in total. Classification uses the same function as the rest of this paper, applied to the pre_tokenizer object extracted from the first 512 kB of each tokenizer.json via an HTTP range request. The vocabulary and merges, which constitute the bulk of the file, are never fetched, so the census consumes a few hundred megabytes rather than several terabytes. Repositories lacking a tokenizer.json are classified from their file layout instead: a SentencePiece model file implies no letter-based pre-tokenization and counts as unaffected, while vocab.json with merges.txt is the pre-tokenizers GPT-2 serialisation, which transformers loads through ByteLevel with the regex enabled, and counts as affected. Dropping either group would bias the result, and the two biases point in opposite directions.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Comparison with released tokenizers
chunks.text:
Dropping either group would bias the result, and the two biases point in opposite directions.

Among text-generation models, 63.3% of the 1,345 classified repositories carry a letters-only pretokenizer. Those repositories account for 52.9% of the 412 distinct tokenizers behind them and 72.5% of 30-day downloads. The three denominators are reported jointly because each is vulnerable to a distinct objection: repository counts inflate whichever base model has the most fine-tunes, distinct-tokenizer counts give a niche tokenizer the same weight as one used by half the ecosystem, and download counts track whatever a few large deployments happen to pull this month. They agree here, which is the useful outcome.

A field whose default is easy to get wrong. HuggingFace's ByteLevel pre-tokenizer applies GPT-2's pattern internally unless use_regex is set to false, and the field is typically absent from the file. GPT-2's own tokenizer.json omits it, and the library fills in true, after which nepālī emerges as six pieces. Reading an absent field as "disabled" would classify the canonical instance of this defect as unaffected, and would do the same for every file written before the field existed. Our classifier treats absence as enabled, matching the library's behaviour; the appendix enumerates the distinct patterns behind these counts.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Comparison with released tokenizers
chunks.text:
Our classifier treats absence as enabled, matching the library's behaviour; the appendix enumerates the distinct patterns behind these counts.

We make no larger claim than the one these counts support: the letters-only word class is what the ecosystem ships by default, not a historical curiosity that has been cleaned up. The Limitations section sets out what the census does not establish.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Which scripts the defect reaches
chunks.text:
pre-tokens under \p{L}+ divided by pre-tokens under [\p{L}\p{M}]+, for all 26 languages on identical content. All 17 abugidas are affected, from 1.47× (Tibetan) to 9.02× (Thai); Latin, Cyrillic, Hangul, and Han sit at exactly 1.00×, since ordinary text in those scripts carries no combining marks after NFC.

Tibetan is a partial exception. At the low end, Tibetan separates syllables with U+0F0B TSHEG (punctuation, Po), which splits under both word classes, so its pre-tokens are syllables either way and the marks merely fragment an already short unit. The defect tracks how much of a word's information Unicode classifies as marks, not whether a script is Brahmic.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Which scripts the defect reaches
chunks.text:
The defect tracks how much of a word's information Unicode classifies as marks, not whether a script is Brahmic.

Arabic and Hebrew are dormant cases. Table 4 reports Arabic at 1.08× and Hebrew at exactly 1.00×, because the evaluation text omits their diacritics, as modern prose does. Vocalised Arabic and pointed Hebrew appear in scripture, poetry, dictionaries, and language-learning material, much of the text a low-resource pipeline is handed. Measured on the same sentence with its marks restored (Table 8, Appendix C), vocalised Arabic shatters 6.50× and pointed Hebrew 6.14×, comparable to Devanagari. A pipeline audited on modern newswire will pass and then fail on the first vocalised corpus it encounters.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Downstream evaluation
chunks.text:
Fertility measures compression. Whether the resulting model is actually better is a separate question.

Design. Two tokenizers split the same text into different numbers of tokens, so per-token loss measures different quantities and cross-tokenizer perplexity is meaningless; every figure here is bits per byte, which normalises by the underlying text. Three runs share an architecture (268M parameters, 16 layers, d model = 1024, context 2048), an optimiser configuration, and a seed. Run A trains the broken tokenizer on N tokens; B trains the fixed tokenizer on the same N ; C trains the broken tokenizer on enough tokens to read the same bytes as B. At a fixed token budget, B reads approximately 3.03× more text than A, so an advantage for B could be attributed to having read more; C eliminates that explanation at a cost of 1.59× B's compute. A and C share one shard set, C's shards being A's read further, so they see identical data in identical order. Evaluation relies on held-out splits disjoint from training: FineWeb-2's designated npi_Deva test split for Nepali, and C4's validation split for English, a different corpus from the FineWeb-Edu the models train on.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Downstream evaluation
chunks.text: Fixing the regex improves the model. At equal compute, B reaches 0.3899 bits per byte on heldout Nepali against A's 0.4080, an improvement of 4.43%. English improves as well, by 1.84%, even though §5 shows the fixed tokenizer costs 2.1% of English fertility. Both arms spend the same token budget, and B's larger tokens mean it reads more text in both languages; the fertility cost is real, yet the downstream effect still runs the other way.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > English is the control channel, and it behaves.
section_path: English is the control channel, and it behaves.
chunks.text:
The regex provably does nothing to Latin script: the shatter ratio is exactly 1.00× ( §8), so B and C segment English into identical pre-tokens and differ only in compute. On English they order by compute, C ahead of B by 1.31%. On Nepali the ordering inverts. B reaches 0.3899 against C's 0.3925 while consuming 63% of C's compute. We state the result in that form deliberately. The raw gap is 0.65% on a single seed with no error bars, which is too thin to defend on its own; the compute-normalised statement does not depend on the gap's magnitude, only on its sign, and the English channel shows what the sign would have been had compute alone been responsible. Read together, the two channels place the benefit beyond compression alone.

What this does not establish. One seed per condition, one model scale, one language pair, and bits per byte rather than task accuracy: a reader who wants a claim about downstream task quality will not find it here. What the three conditions support is narrower, namely that at a fixed compute budget the fixed tokenizer produces a better Nepali model, and that advantage survives handing the broken tokenizer the same bytes and half again as much compute.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Reproducibility
chunks.text:
A single command regenerates every number in this paper, including those quoted in prose: make paper-harness

The harness, the manuscript source, and the released tokenizer are available at https://github.com/sajalregmi/ arkios-tokenizer and https: //huggingface.co/sajalregmi4/ arkios-tokenizer.

It requires no GPU, no HuggingFace account, and no private data. It downloads FLORES-200 as a plain tarball (sha256 b8b0b7678302. . . ), streams a public Nepali-English corpus, trains the matched arms and the sweep, evaluates each tokenizer, and writes a machine-readable results.json together with the L A T E X tables this document includes. A --quick configuration completes in about fifteen minutes and reproduces the bound across 26 languages and the vocalisation probe exactly, since neither depends on the trained arms.

chunks.text:

results.json records the resolved Hub commit of every baseline, the sha256 of every corpus, the version of every library, and the harness's git commit (156f4527); Appendix B provides the corpora, splits, and compute budget in full. Every tokenizer result here ran on a laptop CPU. Only the downstream evaluation ( §9) requires a GPU: three runs totalling 14.36B tokens over 268M-parameter models (2.3×10 19 FLOPs by the 6N D estimate of Kaplan et al., 2020), 19.1 GPU-hours on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5. The census ( §7) is a separate command, because it reads a live service rather than a pinned artifact: rankings and download counts shift, so a rerun will not reproduce our counts exactly, though every repository we classified is recorded in census.json.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Related work
chunks.text: Byte-pair encoding originated as a compression algorithm (Gage, 1994), entered NMT through Sennrich et al. (2016), and became byte-level in Rad- ford et al. (2019), whose pre-tokenization regex is the subject of this paper (Mielke et al., 2021 survey the design space). SentencePiece (Kudo and Richardson, 2018) avoids letter-based pretokenization and the failure that follows from it, at the cost of the fidelity issues our measurements reveal; tokenizer-free models sidestep the question entirely by operating on bytes or characters (Xue et al., 2022;Clark et al., 2022), at a compute cost byte-level BPE exists to avoid. Indic tokenization has received targeted attention, including the IndicNLP suite (Kakwani et al., 2020), and massively multilingual models have long contended with script diversity (Conneau et al., 2020); Devanagari fragmentation under English-centric tokenizers has been observed before.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Related work
chunks.text: Tokenizer quality outside English is well documented. Rust et al. (2021) Closest to this work, Velayuthan and Sarveswaran (2025) identify pre-tokenization as the source of unfair representation for Tamil, Sinhala, and Hindi and propose Grapheme Pair Encoding, segmenting on graphemes rather than bytes. We agree on the diagnosis and differ on what follows from it: they introduce and evaluate a new segmentation algorithm; we quantify what the existing defect costs under a one-variable control, derive the bound that explains why the cost resists corpus composition, provide a diagnostic that identifies the failure without reading the pre-tokenizer, and measure both the downstream effect and the defect's prevalence across the deployed ecosystem. GPE changes the segmentation unit; the repair we measure is a one-character-class edit that leaves byte-level BPE intact and is already present in o200k.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Conclusion
chunks.text:
A character class chosen for English places a floor under Nepali tokenization that Nepali data cannot lift. The floor follows from the pre-tokenizer rather than from measurement: BPE cannot merge across pre-token boundaries, so a regex that splits words at every vowel sign bounds fertility before training begins. On parallel text the effect reaches every abugida we tested and lies dormant in vocalised Arabic and pointed Hebrew.

The floor is also tight. Across 5 matched pairs spanning 2.2× in predicted effect, every control arm settles within 2.2% of what a regex match predicts before any training, which makes the bound a design-time check rather than a post-hoc explanation. Yet the word class it checks for remains the ecosystem's default, present in 63.3% of the most-downloaded text-generation repositories on the HuggingFace Hub. Repairing it takes one character class, and the repair was already known. The diagnostic generalises further than the defect does: a metric that will not respond to the input that supposedly drives it is constrained somewhere else, and in a tokenizer pipeline the candidates upstream of the corpus number three: the normaliser, the pre-tokenizer, and the vocabulary budget.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Limitations
chunks.text:
The repair is prior art. o200k already employs a mark-aware word class. Our contribution lies in measurement, diagnosis, and scope.

5 trained language pairs, not 26. The bound in §8 spans 26 languages and requires no training. The trained pairs cover 5: Hindi, Bengali, Nepali, Tamil and Malayalam. Thai, Khmer, Lao, Myanmar, and Tibetan are absent from the trained set; they are also the languages where fertility is undefined and the bound is hardest to interpret. The sweep in §4 is Nepali-English only.

Every trained pair is 50/50 with English. The four new pairs fix the target-language byte share at 50%, far above what a general-purpose multilingual tokenizer would allocate to any single language. That choice keeps the five pairs comparable to each other and to the Nepali pair, and the sweep confirms the control arm is insensitive to the share; it does mean the treatment fertilities exceed what a realistic multilingual mixture would yield, and the control-to-treatment ratios are correspondingly optimistic.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Limitations
chunks.text:
The census measures exposure. §7 counts repositories whose pre-tokenizer is letters-only. It does not establish that any of them is harmed by it: for a model that only ever processes Latin script, the word class is irrelevant. It is also a snapshot of a live ranking, taken once, and it excludes gated repositories along with every repository that ships no tokenizer.json. The language-tag restriction depends on repository metadata that authors maintain unevenly.

Translated evaluation text. FLORES-200 (NLLB Team et al., 2022) is translated from English-sourced Wikimedia articles. Its parallelism is what makes cross-language comparison valid, and it is cleaner and more uniform than native web text. The harness also supports a secondary evaluation on native FineWeb-2 text.

Whitespace words. Tokens per whitespacedelimited word is a coarse measure for morphologically rich languages and undefined for scripts without inter-word spaces. We report tokens per 100 characters alongside it and omit fertility where it would mislead.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Limitations
chunks.text:
We report tokens per 100 characters alongside it and omit fertility where it would mislead.

One seed per downstream condition. §9 trains each of A, B, and C once, at one model scale, and reports bits per byte rather than task accuracy. The B-C gap on Nepali is 0.65%, too small to separate from seed variance on a single run; we therefore state that comparison in compute-normalised form, where the conclusion depends on the sign rather than the magnitude. Repeated seeds, a second model scale, and downstream task evaluation would all strengthen the section, and we have not run them.

chunks.text: fixed. The English cost in §5 follows from that choice and would shrink at a larger vocabulary. We have not mapped the trade-off.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > Ethical Considerations
chunks.text:
The defect this paper measures is not distributed evenly. Its cost falls entirely on languages written in abugida scripts and, when diacritics are present, on Arabic and Hebrew. For Latin, Cyrillic, Hangul, and Han the shatter ratio is exactly 1.00×, so speakers of those languages could not have noticed the problem from their own usage. Because fertility translates directly into context length, training cost, and per-token API price, a defect of this shape widens an existing gap between well-resourced and low-resourced languages while remaining invisible to the people best placed to correct it.

The failure mode compounds that asymmetry. It presents as a data shortage, the explanation practitioners working on low-resource languages already expect and the one they are most likely to act on. Effort then goes into acquiring text that cannot help, and the misattribution is most expensive where budgets are smallest.

We see no dual-use concern in this work. The evaluation corpora are public and contain no personal data. The tokenizer we release is trained on public web text alongside a private custom corpus that we do not redistribute, and it inherits whatever biases those sources carry; we make no claim that it is suitable for deployment without further evaluation. Every experimental result in this paper, including the matched pair, the sweep, and the downstream ablation, uses only public data, so none of them depends on the private corpus.

chunks.text: results.json records the resolved Hub commit of each baseline tokenizer, the sha256 of each corpus, the version of each library, and the harness's git commit (156f4527). Three baselines load from widely used republications of a gated upstream, allowing the harness to run without an account; each is annotated with its source. The FineWeb-2 evaluation slice and the tokenizer training corpus are partitioned by document index modulo 20, disjoint at any corpus size. Training corpora are FineWeb-2 (Penedo et al., 2025) for each non-English language and FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) for English; the downstream English validation set is the validation split of C4 (Raffel et al., 2020), distinct from the corpus those models train on. The census ( §7) runs as a separate command, python -m tokenizer.paper.census, because it reads a live service rather than a pinned artifact: rankings and download counts shift, so a rerun will not reproduce our counts exactly, though every repository we classified is recorded in census.json.

chunks.header: Vowel Signs Are Not Letters: A Pre-tokenization Ceiling on Multilingual Tokenizer Fertility > B Corpora, splits and compute budget
section_path: B Corpora, splits and compute budget
chunks.text: Computational budget. Every tokenizer result in this paper ran on a laptop CPU: a single 65,536entry BPE over the 2000 MB corpus takes one to eight minutes; the 5 matched pairs and the 7point sweep in both arms amount to 24 tokenizers, roughly three hours total, dominated by streaming rather than training; the 26-language bound and the vocalisation probe require no training and finish in seconds; the census is network-bound, 3,479 range requests in roughly fifteen minutes. Only the downstream evaluation ( §9) requires a GPU: the three runs total 14.36B tokens over 268Mparameter models (2.3 × 10 19 FLOPs by the 6N D estimate of Kaplan et al., 2020) and took 19.1 GPUhours on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5 (5.3 h each for A and B, 8.5 h for C) using a custom C/CUDA trainer in bf16 with cuDNN fused attention at 34% of peak FLOPs. Two classes of repository are excluded from each denominator in Table 3: those that ship no tokenizer of any kind (797 of the overall top-2,000 listing, comprising vision, audio, and diffusion models, plus quantised redistributions that carry weights only), and gated repositories alongside the handful whose pre_tokenizer did not fit in an 8 MB range request. Neither is folded into the affected or the unaffected side, because doing so would shift the headline number with no evidence behind it. What is deliberately not excluded is the group that ships a tokenizer in some older or nontokenizers format. Excluding those would bias the result twice over and in opposite directions: SentencePiece repositories are definitively unaffected, so dropping them raises the letters-only share, while repositories carrying vocab.json and merges.txt without a tokenizer.json are definitively affected, since that pair is GPT-2's original serialisation and transformers loads it through ByteLevel with the regex enabled, so dropping them lowers it. Both are classified from their file layout, which resolves the question without downloading anything.

Figure 2 plots each arm's own training-free bound ( §3) against the fertility that arm actually attains, for all 5 matched pairs of §5 and both arms of each.

Proposition 1 forces every one of the ten points onto or above the dashed line and says nothing further. What the theorem does not force is the difference between the two series: the control arm lies on the line across the entire range, while the treatment arm lies well above its own much lower floor. That difference is the practical content of the bound. chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Abstract
chunks.text: Large language models (LLMs) do not read words; they read tokens, and the tokenizer decides how many tokens a language needs to say the same thing.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Abstract
chunks.text: This paper introduces the notion of a Sindhi token tax and tests it empirically for Pakistan's English-Sindhi context. Using 1,004 parallel sentences from the FLORES-200 benchmark in English, Sindhi and Urdu, the study measured five widely deployed tokenizers (GPT-2, Llama 2, Llama 3, Qwen2 and Command-R) with a reproducible Python pipeline. A convergent mixed-methods design combined quantitative indices with a rule-assisted qualitative analysis of how frequent Sindhi words are segmented. Quantitatively, Sindhi required 2.87 to 4.98 times as many tokens as English for the same content in total (Wilcoxon signed-rank, r = .87, p < .001), and a 4,096-token context window held about 770 to 1,335 Sindhi words against 2,890 to 3,330 English words. A new Orthographic Penalty Index showed that the 18 letters unique to the Sindhi alphabet, such as ‫,ڪ‬ ‫,ٿ‬ ‫ڻ‬ and ‫,ڳ‬ were split into byte fragments in 100% of their occurrences in four of the five tokenizers, while letters shared with Arabic and Urdu were almost never split. Qualitatively, five patterns emerged, including the fragmentation of core grammatical words, the "Urdu shortcut" by which Urdu code points are cheaper than Sindhi ones, and the invisibility of Sindhi morphology to subword boundaries. The study also found Unicode inconsistency in digital Sindhi, with 238 of 1,004 benchmark sentences mixing forms of the letter heh. The paper proposes the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF) and argues that script-level design, not only data scarcity, makes AI costlier and weaker for Sindhi speakers, with implications for language policy, education and technology in Pakistan.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Introduction Background
chunks.text: Computational linguistics in the 2020s is dominated by large language models. Systems built on transformer architectures now translate, summarise, tutor and converse in dozens of languages, and they are rapidly entering classrooms, offices and public services across South Asia (Dubey et al., 2024;Touvron et al., 2023;Yang et al., 2024). Behind every such system sits a component that users rarely see: the tokenizer. Before a model can process a sentence, the tokenizer cuts it into units called tokens, drawn from a fixed vocabulary learned mainly from the data on which the model was trained (Kudo & Richardson, 2018;Sennrich et al., 2016). The number of tokens a sentence needs determines how much it costs to process, how much of it fits into the model's context window, and, indirectly, how well the model learns the language (Mielke et al., 2021;Rust et al., 2021).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Introduction Background
chunks.text: Because tokenizer vocabularies are learned from data dominated by English and a small number of other high-resource languages, they encode English efficiently and many other languages inefficiently. Petrov et al. (2023) showed that the same text can require many times more tokens in some languages than in English, and Ahia et al. (2023) demonstrated that speakers of such languages pay more for commercial language-model services while receiving poorer results. Global surveys of language technology confirm that the benefits of NLP are distributed very unevenly across the world's languages (Blasi et al., 2022;Joshi et al., 2020;Ranathunga & de Silva, 2022).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Introduction Background
chunks.text: The Pakistani context: English and Sindhi Pakistan is a multilingual country in which English holds the highest institutional prestige, Urdu serves as the national language, and regional languages such as Sindhi, Punjabi, Pashto and Balochi carry the everyday lives of millions (Mansoor, 2005;Rahman, 1996Rahman, , 2002)). Sindhi is the language of Sindh province, has official status there, and possesses a long literary and journalistic tradition; it is spoken by tens of millions of people (Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, 2023;Rahman, 1996). In computational terms, however, Sindhi is a low-resource language. Its digital corpora, annotated datasets and language tools remain limited compared with English and even Urdu (Ali et al., 2019;Jamro, 2017;Motlani, 2016).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Introduction Background
chunks.text:
Sindhi is written in a Perso-Arabic script that extends the Arabic alphabet with letters for sounds that Arabic, Persian and Urdu lack: implosives such as ‫,ٻ‬ ‫,ڄ‬ ‫ڳ‬ and ‫,ڏ‬ retroflex consonants such as ‫,ٽ‬ ‫ڊ‬ and ‫,ڻ‬ aspirated forms such as ‫ٿ‬ and ‫,ڀ‬ and distinctive letters such as ‫ڪ‬ (Unicode Consortium, 2023). These letters are central to Sindhi grammar and vocabulary; the everyday verb ‫رڻ‬ ‫ڪ‬ (to do) contains two of them. If a tokenizer's vocabulary contains the Arabic and Urdu letters but not the Sindhi ones, Sindhi text will be penalised at the most basic level of the writing system. This paper calls that penalty the orthographic penalty, and the extra cost it produces the Sindhi token tax.

Pakistan's own policy agenda gives the question urgency. The Digital Pakistan Policy commits the state to digital inclusion and e-services for all citizens (Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, 2018). If AI services cost more and work worse in Sindhi than in English, digital inclusion will reproduce the old linguistic hierarchy in a new technological form (Bender et al., 2021;Rahman, 2002).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > The problem
chunks.text:
Existing studies of tokenization inequity treat languages in large multilingual samples and rarely examine the internal structure of particular scripts (Ahia et al., 2023;Petrov et al., 2023). Research on Sindhi computational linguistics has concentrated on corpora, part-of-speech tagging, word embeddings and spell checking (Ali et al., 2019;Jamro, 2017;Motlani, 2016) rather than on how contemporary LLM tokenizers treat the language. No study, to the author's knowledge, has measured the tokenization of Sindhi against English and Urdu across several modern LLM tokenizers, or asked which features of the Sindhi script drive the cost.

The new idea This paper advances three original contributions. First, it proposes the concept of the Sindhi token tax: the extra computational and economic cost that a Sindhi speaker incurs, relative to an English speaker, for communicating the same content with an LLM. Second, it introduces the Orthographic Penalty Index (OPI), a script-level measure that compares the fragmentation of letters unique to a language's alphabet with the fragmentation of letters it shares with better-resourced languages. Third, it proposes the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF), which links orthographic, segmentation, economic and representational equity in a single cascade.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > The problem
chunks.text:
Third, it proposes the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF), which links orthographic, segmentation, economic and representational equity in a single cascade.

Research questions 1. RQ1. How large is the token premium for Sindhi relative to English, and to Urdu, across contemporary LLM tokenizers? 2. RQ2. To what extent do letters unique to the Sindhi alphabet drive fragmentation, as measured by the Orthographic Penalty Index? 3. RQ3. How do tokenizers segment frequent Sindhi words, and what linguistic patterns does this segmentation reveal? 4. RQ4. What are the implications for AI access, language policy and education in Pakistan?

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Significance
chunks.text: The study contributes to computational linguistics by adding a script-level dimension to the measurement of tokenization inequity, and to English linguistics in Pakistan by showing how the dominance of English is being reproduced inside the architecture of AI systems. Because the analysis uses an open benchmark and public tokenizer vocabularies, every figure in this paper can be reproduced by other researchers (Goyal et al., 2022;NLLB Team et al., 2022).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Review of Literature From words to subwords
section_path: Review of Literature From words to subwords
chunks.text:
Early statistical NLP operated on whole words, which forced systems to treat any unseen word as unknown. Sennrich et al. (2016) adapted byte-pair encoding (BPE) to neural machine translation: starting from characters, the algorithm repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols until it reaches a target vocabulary size. Kudo (2018) proposed the unigram languagemodel tokenizer, and Kudo and Richardson (2018) released SentencePiece, which treats text as a raw stream of Unicode characters and has become the standard toolkit for multilingual models.

GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE, in which the base alphabet is the 256 possible bytes of UTF-8, so that any string can be encoded without unknown tokens (Radford et al., 2019). Mielke et al. (2021) review this history and note that subword tokenization is a compromise: it guarantees coverage, but the resulting segments need not correspond to meaningful linguistic units.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Tokenizer quality and model performance
chunks.text: Tokenization is not a neutral pre-processing step. Rust et al. (2021) showed that multilingual models perform worse on languages whose tokenizers produce high fertility, the average number of tokens per word, and that replacing a multilingual tokenizer with a dedicated monolingual one improves downstream results. Limisiewicz et al. (2023) found that the way vocabulary is allocated across languages affects multilingual performance, and Liang et al. (2023) showed that simply enlarging the vocabulary to one million tokens (XLM-V) benefits low-resource languages. At the other extreme, Xue et al. (2022) proposed ByT5, a token-free model operating directly on bytes, which is robust to spelling variation but computationally expensive because sequences become long.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Tokenizer quality and model performance
chunks.text: Tokenization as an equity problem A recent line of research reframes tokenization as a matter of fairness. Petrov et al. (2023) compared 17 tokenizers on the parallel FLORES-200 corpus and found that some languages need more than ten times as many tokens as English for the same text, which they call a premium; they recommend that tokenizers be trained to achieve parity across languages. Ahia et al. (2023) showed that commercial APIs charge by the token, so speakers of high-premium languages pay more for the same service and fit less text into the model's context. These findings connect to broader critiques of language technology: Joshi et al. (2020) classified most of the world's languages as "left behind" by NLP resources, Blasi et al. (2022) documented systematic performance gaps across languages that correlate with economic and demographic power, and Bender et al. (2021) warned that the costs and risks of large models fall unevenly on marginalised communities.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Scripts, Unicode and byte fragmentation
chunks.text: Most equity studies measure tokens per sentence without asking why some languages fragment more. One reason lies in the script. In UTF-8, Latin letters take one byte, whereas Arabic-script letters take two bytes (Unicode Consortium, 2023). A byte-level tokenizer that has not learned a merged token for a particular Arabic-script letter must represent it as two separate byte tokens, neither of which is a meaningful character (Radford et al., 2019;Xue et al., 2022). SentencePiece tokenizers face a parallel problem through byte fallback: characters outside the learned vocabulary are encoded as raw bytes (Kudo & Richardson, 2018). The Arabic block of Unicode contains many letters used only by particular languages, including the Sindhi letters in the range U+0680 to U+06BF, and these are likely to be rare in training data dominated by Arabic, Persian and Urdu. The script, therefore, can impose a penalty on top of the general scarcity of data.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Scripts, Unicode and byte fragmentation
chunks.text:
The script, therefore, can impose a penalty on top of the general scarcity of data.

Computational linguistics for Sindhi and Urdu in Pakistan Urdu language processing in Pakistan has developed through sustained institutional work on corpora, lexicons and tools (Hussain, 2008). Sindhi has received less attention. Jamro (2017) surveyed Sindhi language processing and identified the scarcity of annotated corpora, script complexity and the coexistence of Perso-Arabic and Devanagari writing as major obstacles. Motlani (2016) described the development of basic tools such as tokenisers and morphological resources for Sindhi and characterised it as a resource-poor language. Ali et al. (2019) built a large Sindhi corpus from news and web sources and trained word embeddings, noting the need to normalise inconsistent spellings and character encodings. Multilingual benchmarks have since begun to include Sindhi: FLORES-200 provides professionally translated sentences in more than 200 languages, including Sindhi in Arabic script (Goyal et al., 2022;NLLB Team et al., 2022), and SIB-200 adds topic labels to the same sentences (Adelani et al., 2024). Language policy research, however, reminds us that the digital fate of Sindhi is shaped by the same hierarchy that places English above Urdu and Urdu above regional languages in Pakistani institutions (Mansoor, 2005;Rahman, 1996Rahman, , 2002)).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Research gap
chunks.text: Three gaps follow from this review. First, tokenization-equity studies have not examined Sindhi specifically or compared it with both English and Urdu within the Pakistani context. Second, no study has isolated the contribution of language-specific letters to tokenization cost. Third, there is no framework that connects script-level encoding with segmentation, cost and representation in a way that can guide policy for a multilingual country such as Pakistan.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Theoretical framework: the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF)
section_path: Theoretical framework: the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF)
chunks.text:
This paper proposes the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF) as an original synthesis of the literature reviewed above. It organises tokenization equity into four layers, arranged as a cascade from the writing system upward (Figure 1). Layer 2, Segmentation equity, asks how many tokens a word needs, how often frequent words are kept whole, and whether token boundaries respect morphological structure (Kudo & Richardson, 2018;Rust et al., 2021;Sennrich et al., 2016).

Layer 3, Economic equity, asks how much more a speaker pays per message and how much less text fits into a model's context window (Ahia et al., 2023;Petrov et al., 2023).

Layer 4, Representational equity, asks whether the resulting models serve the language community with comparable quality, visibility and trust (Bender et al., 2021;Blasi et al., 2022;Joshi et al., 2020).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Theoretical framework: the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF)
section_path: Theoretical framework: the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF)
chunks.text: The arrow in Figure 1 expresses the framework's central claim: inequity introduced at the orthographic layer propagates upward. Fragmented letters produce more tokens per word; more tokens per word mean higher costs and shorter effective context; and higher costs and poorer segmentation contribute to weaker, more expensive AI for the language community. SATEF adds three diagnostic indices: the Token Premium (TP), the Orthographic Penalty Index (OPI) and the Whole-Word Rate (WWR). The present study measures Layers 1 to 3 directly and discusses Layer 4 on the basis of prior research.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Research Methodology
chunks.text:
Research design

The study follows a convergent mixed-methods design in which a quantitative computational experiment and a qualitative analysis of segmentation are conducted separately and integrated at the interpretation stage (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). The quantitative strand measures token counts, fertility, fragmentation and the OPI across languages and tokenizers. The qualitative strand examines how individual Sindhi words are segmented and interprets the patterns linguistically, using a codebook and rule-assisted coding followed by close reading (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Tokenizers
chunks.text: Five tokenizers were selected to represent the main families and generations of LLM tokenization (Table 2). Their vocabularies were obtained from public sources: the GGUF vocabulary files distributed with the open-source llama.cpp project (ggml-org, 2024) and the SentencePiece model released with the llama2.c project (Karpathy, 2023). Byte-level BPE tokenizers were reconstructed with the Hugging Face tokenizers library (Wolf et al., 2020) from their published vocabularies, merge lists and pre-tokenization rules; the Llama 2 tokenizer was run directly with SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018). As a validity check, the control phrase Hello world was encoded with the reference token identifiers of the original tokenizers (for example, 15496 and 995 for GPT-2, and 9906 and 1917 for Llama 3). For Command-R, whose pre-tokenization rules are not fully documented, the GPT-2 splitting rule was used; this rule affects digits and punctuation rather than Arabic-script letters, so its effect on Sindhi counts is negligible. Quantitative measures Six measures were computed for every sentence, language and tokenizer. Tokens per sentence is the raw count.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Tokenizers
chunks.text:
Quantitative measures Six measures were computed for every sentence, language and tokenizer. Tokens per sentence is the raw count. Token premium (TP) is the number of tokens for a Sindhi (or Urdu) sentence divided by the number for its English equivalent (Petrov et al., 2023). Fertility is the number of tokens per whitespace-separated word (Rust et al., 2021). Effective context capacity is the number of words that fit into a 4,096-token window, calculated as 4,096 divided by fertility (Ahia et al., 2023). Fragmentation rate is the percentage of non-space characters whose UTF-8 bytes are divided between two or more tokens. The Orthographic Penalty Index (OPI) is the fragmentation rate of the 18 letters unique to the Sindhi alphabet ‫ٻ(‬ ‫ڀ‬ ‫ٽ‬ ‫ٺ‬ ‫ٿ‬ ‫ڄ‬ ‫ڃ‬ ‫ڇ‬ ‫ڌ‬ ‫ڏ‬ ‫ڊ‬ ‫ڍ‬ ‫ڙ‬ ‫ڦ‬ ‫ڪ‬ ‫ڳ‬ ‫ڱ‬ ‫)ڻ‬ minus the fragmentation rate of 32 letters Sindhi shares with the Arabic, Persian and Urdu alphabets, measured over their occurrences in running Sindhi text:

OPI = 𝐹 Sindhi-specific -𝐹 shared

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Tokenizers
chunks.text:
OPI = 𝐹 Sindhi-specific -𝐹 shared

An OPI of 0 means Sindhi's own letters are treated like shared letters; an OPI of 100 means every occurrence of a Sindhi-specific letter is fragmented while no shared letter is. Letter-level encoding was also tested in isolation. Finally, the Sindhi corpus was scanned for alternative Unicode code points for the letters heh and yeh.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Statistical analysis
chunks.text: Because token premiums are ratios with skewed distributions, non-parametric tests were used. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests compared paired Sindhi and English, and Sindhi and Urdu, token counts for each tokenizer, with effect size r = z/√N (Wilcoxon, 1945;Cohen, 1988). A Friedman test compared the Sindhi premium across the five tokenizers, with Kendall's W as effect size (Friedman, 1937). A Kruskal-Wallis test compared the premium across the seven topic domains, and chisquare tests compared the fragmentation of Sindhi and Urdu characters.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Qualitative strand
chunks.text: The 80 most frequent Sindhi word types in the corpus (excluding numerals and Latin-script tokens) were segmented by each tokenizer, giving 400 segmentations. Each was coded with a five-category codebook (Table 5): whole word; morph-aligned, where a word is split into full characters and the final piece matches a Sindhi inflectional ending such as ‫,ڻ-‬ ‫,ن-‬ ‫,و-‬ ‫ي-‬ or ‫;ا-‬ arbitrary sub-word; character-level; and byte-fragmented, where at least one piece is a partial character. A first pass was applied automatically by rules, after which the segmentations were read closely and interpreted, following the familiarisation, coding and theme-generation phases of thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). One representative sentence was also visualised across all tokenizers.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Software and reproducibility
chunks.text: The pipeline was written in Python 3, using pandas for data management (McKinney, 2010), SciPy for statistics (Virtanen et al., 2020), Matplotlib for charts (Hunter, 2007), the tokenizers library (Wolf et al., 2020), SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018), and the Pillow imaging library with the libraqm text-layout engine to render correctly shaped Sindhi script. All data and vocabularies are public, and the scripts accompany this paper, so every result can be regenerated.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Ethical considerations
chunks.text: The study analyses published benchmark sentences and public software artefacts; it involves no human participants and no personal data. The FLORES-200 and SIB-200 datasets are released under open licences for research use (Adelani et al., 2024;NLLB Team et al., 2022).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text:
All results in this section were computed with the Python pipeline described in Section 3. Quantitative interpretation of Figure 2. For English, all five tokenizers needed between 26 and 30 tokens per sentence on average. For Sindhi, GPT-2 needed 132 tokens and Llama 2 needed 128, while the three 2024 tokenizers needed 76 to 77. Urdu followed a similar pattern at a slightly higher level (83 to 167 tokens). In total, the 1,004 English sentences required 26,513 to 30,563 tokens, whereas the same sentences in Sindhi required 75,990 to 132,374 tokens (Table 3).

Qualitative reading of Figure 2. English is encoded almost identically by every tokenizer, from 2019 to 2024, which shows that English efficiency was already solved in the earliest model. Sindhi improved substantially between the older and newer tokenizers, yet even the best 2024 tokenizers need about three tokens for every English one. Progress for Sindhi has been real but incomplete, and it has come as a side effect of larger multilingual vocabularies rather than deliberate design for the language (Dubey et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2024). The token premium line.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text:
The token premium line.

Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirmed that Sindhi needed more tokens than English in every tokenizer (z = 27.45, p < .001, r = .87; Table 4); in fact every one of the 1,004 Sindhi sentences needed more tokens than its English equivalent. A Friedman test showed that the premium differed strongly across tokenizers, χ²(4) = 3,238.19, p < .001, Kendall's W = .81. Urdu's median premium was slightly higher than Sindhi's (3.09 to 6.32), and Sindhi sentences needed fewer tokens than Urdu ones in all five tokenizers (median differences of 5 to 32 tokens). Note. All p < .001. For Sindhi vs English, every sentence pair showed a positive difference, so z reaches the same ceiling value in all tokenizers.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text:
Note. All p < .001. For Sindhi vs English, every sentence pair showed a positive difference, so z reaches the same ceiling value in all tokenizers.

Qualitative reading of Figure 3. The premium is best understood as a price. If a service charges by the token, a Sindhi speaker pays roughly three times as much as an English speaker for the same message with current tokenizers, and five times as much with GPT-2 (Ahia et al., 2023;Petrov et al., 2023). This is the Sindhi token tax. The comparison with Urdu is revealing: Sindhi is not worse than Urdu at the sentence level, partly because the Urdu translations are longer (27,447 words against 24,767). The disadvantage both languages share is relative to English, which reflects the Englishcentred composition of training data and the prestige hierarchy of Pakistani languages (Joshi et al., 2020;Rahman, 2002).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text:
The disadvantage both languages share is relative to English, which reflects the Englishcentred composition of training data and the prestige hierarchy of Pakistani languages (Joshi et al., 2020;Rahman, 2002).

Fertility and effective context Quantitative interpretation of Figure 4. English fertility was almost constant at 1.23 to 1.42 tokens per word. Sindhi fertility fell from 5.35 (GPT-2) and 5.21 (Llama 2) to 3.07 to 3.14 in the 2024 tokenizers, closely tracking Urdu. In a 4,096-token context window, a model can therefore hold about 3,300 English words but only 766 to 1,335 Sindhi words. Put differently, a Sindhi reader receives between 23% and 40% of the context capacity an English reader receives.

Qualitative reading of Figure 4. Context capacity determines what an AI system can "see" at once: a long legal document, a school textbook chapter or a conversation history. A Sindhi user who wants a model to summarise a document, answer questions about a policy text or keep track of a long tutoring dialogue runs out of context roughly three times sooner than an English user. For education in Sindh, where textbooks and assessments are produced in Sindhi, this is a practical limitation, not merely a technical statistic (Rust et al., 2021).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text:
For education in Sindh, where textbooks and assessments are produced in Sindhi, this is a practical limitation, not merely a technical statistic (Rust et al., 2021).

Character fragmentation residual fragmentation must therefore come from something Sindhi has and Urdu does not, which points directly to the letters unique to the Sindhi alphabet. The next two figures test this explanation. Sindhi letters in isolation (RQ2) Figure 6. Tokens needed to encode each letter in isolation Quantitative interpretation of Figure 6. Each cell shows how many tokens a single letter needs. In GPT-2, Llama 2, Llama 3 and Command-R, every one of the 18 Sindhi-specific letters needed two tokens, meaning none exists as a whole token in these vocabularies (0% single-token coverage). Shared letters were whole in almost every case (96.9% to 100% in the newer tokenizers; 40.6% in GPT-2). Qwen2 was the exception: it encoded 12 of the 18 Sindhi-specific letters (66.7%) as single tokens, but still fragmented six, including ‫,ڻ‬ ‫ٽ‬ and ‫.ڏ‬ Qualitative reading of Figure 6. The dividing line in the heat map is not a line between rich and poor languages; it is a line inside a single script. The letters that Sindhi shares with Arabic, Persian and Urdu are protected by those languages' presence in training data. The letters that belong to Sindhi alone are left out. The fact that Qwen2 includes most of them shows that this is a design outcome, not a technical necessity (Kudo & Richardson, 2018; Liang et al., 2023). The Orthographic Penalty Index Figure 7. Fragmentation of Sindhi-specific and shared letters in running text, and the resulting OPI

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text:
The Orthographic Penalty Index Figure 7. Fragmentation of Sindhi-specific and shared letters in running text, and the resulting OPI

Quantitative interpretation of Figure 7. Sindhi-specific letters make up 11.9% of all letter occurrences in the Sindhi corpus. In Llama 2, Llama 3 and Command-R, 100% of those occurrences were fragmented, while 0% of shared letters were, giving the maximum OPI of 100. GPT-2 fragmented all Sindhi-specific letters and a quarter of shared ones (OPI = 74.8). Qwen2 fragmented 35.9% of Sindhi-specific letter occurrences and almost no shared letters (OPI = 35.9).

Qualitative reading of Figure 7. The OPI isolates a penalty that general measures such as the premium cannot show. Even in the tokenizers where Sindhi's premium is lowest, the language's own letters are systematically broken, while its borrowed letters are not. In SATEF terms, this is inequity at Layer 1, the orthographic foundation, and every higher layer inherits it: each fragmented letter adds a token, and each added token raises cost and shortens context.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text: Does the premium vary by topic? Unicode variation in digital Sindhi Figure 9. (a) Code points used for heh and yeh in the Sindhi corpus; (b) token cost of the same word written with two different code points Quantitative interpretation of Figure 9. The Sindhi benchmark text used the Arabic heh (U+0647) 4,794 times, the do-chashmi heh (U+06BE) 49 times, and the Urdu heh goal (U+06C1) 397 times; 238 of the 1,004 sentences mixed the Urdu heh goal with another heh. The Arabic yeh (U+064A) was used 12,558 times and the Farsi/Urdu yeh (U+06CC) 8 times. The same word te ‫ه(‬ ‫,ت‬ "that, then") cost one token in Llama 3 and Command-R when written with U+0647, but three tokens when written with U+06C1 ‫ہ(‬ ‫;)ت‬ the same held for be ‫ه(‬ ‫ہ/ب‬ ‫,ب‬ "also").

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Data Collection and Analysis
chunks.text: Qualitative reading of Figure 9. Digital Sindhi is not yet orthographically stable. Writers and keyboards mix Sindhi, Urdu and Arabic code points for what readers perceive as the same letter, so a tokenizer sees two different words where a reader sees one (Ali et al., 2019;Unicode Consortium, 2023). This doubles the vocabulary Sindhi needs, splits its statistics, and makes each variant rarer and more fragmented. It should be noted that not all apparent variation is error: the letter ‫,ک‬ which represents /k/ in Urdu, is a distinct Sindhi letter for the aspirated /kʰ/, and its 998 occurrences in the corpus are legitimate.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Part B: Qualitative Analysis
chunks.text:
Segmentation typology (RQ3) Qualitative reading of Figure 10. For English, the most common words of the language are the cheapest units in the model. For Sindhi, even the commonest words are built from fragments. Only a handful of morph-aligned segmentations appear anywhere, which means that token boundaries rarely coincide with the grammatical structure a Sindhi speaker would recognise.

One sentence, five tokenizers

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Qualitative themes
chunks.text:
Close reading of the 400 coded segmentations produced five interpretive themes.

Theme 1: The grammar is in fragments. The words most frequently broken into bytes are not rare terms but the core of Sindhi grammar: the light verbs and auxiliaries ‫ري‬ ‫ڪ‬ (doing), ‫يو‬ ‫ڪ‬ (did), ‫ئي‬ ‫ڪ‬ (did, feminine), ‫و‬ ‫,ٿ‬ ‫ي‬ ‫ٿ‬ and ‫ا‬ ‫ٿ‬ (present-tense auxiliaries) and the verb ‫رڻ‬ ‫ڪ‬ (to do). In GPT-2, Llama 2, Llama 3 and Command-R, ‫رڻ‬ ‫ڪ‬ becomes five tokens, four of which are half-letters. A model trained on such input must learn the most basic verbal system of Sindhi from pieces that carry no linguistic meaning on their own (Mielke et al., 2021).

Theme 2: Borrowed efficiency. Where Sindhi words consist only of letters shared with Urdu, Persian and Arabic, the newer tokenizers treat them well: ‫,جي‬ ‫جو‬ and ‫جا‬ (genitive markers), ‫ان‬ ‫ک‬ (from), ‫سان‬ (with), ‫طور‬ (manner) and ‫عام‬ (common) are single tokens in Llama 3 and Command-R. Sindhi's efficiency is therefore borrowed from its neighbours. It benefits where it overlaps with betterresourced languages and is penalised where it is itself.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Qualitative themes
chunks.text:
Sindhi's efficiency is therefore borrowed from its neighbours. It benefits where it overlaps with betterresourced languages and is penalised where it is itself.

Theme 3: The Urdu shortcut. Because Urdu code points are better represented, spelling a Sindhi word with an Urdu letter can make it cheaper, and spelling it with the standard Sindhi letter makes it costlier (Figure 9). The tokenizer thus creates a small but persistent incentive toward Urdushaped spelling. In a language whose orthography is already unstable online, such incentives could, over time, reinforce the drift of digital Sindhi toward Urdu conventions, a technological echo of the language hierarchy described by Rahman (1996Rahman ( , 2002)).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Qualitative themes
chunks.text:
Theme 4: Morphology out of sight. Sindhi marks infinitives with ‫,ڻ-‬ plural and oblique forms with -‫,ن‬ and gender and number agreement with ‫,و-‬ ‫ي-‬ and ‫.ا-‬ These endings rarely become token boundaries. The infinitive ending ‫ڻ‬ is itself a Sindhi-specific letter, so it is always split into bytes except where it is absorbed into a longer piece. The agreement paradigm ‫,جو‬ ‫,جي‬ ‫جا‬ appears as three unrelated whole tokens rather than as one stem with three endings. Only occasionally, as in ‫نجي‬ ‫نه‬ ‫پ‬ (one's own, feminine), does the final token coincide with an agreement ending. A model therefore receives little help from its input in learning Sindhi morphology (Rust et al., 2021).

Theme 5: Coverage is a choice. Qwen2 shows what changes when Sindhi letters are added to the vocabulary: ‫و‬ ‫ٿ‬ becomes ‫ٿ‬ | ‫,و‬ and byte fragmentation almost disappears. But Qwen2's words are then segmented mostly letter by letter, and its overall premium (2.86) is no lower than that of Llama 3. Adding letters removes the orthographic penalty but not the segmentation penalty; for that, a tokenizer needs Sindhi text in its training data so that frequent Sindhi letter sequences are merged into larger units (Liang et al., 2023;Sennrich et al., 2016).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Discussion
chunks.text: Integrating the strands Table 6 brings the two strands together, layer by layer, following the logic of the SATEF framework (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). Inferred: fragmented input weakens learning (Rust et al., 2021) Answering the research questions RQ1 asked how large the Sindhi token premium is. It is large and universal: a median of 2.85 to 4.98 times the English token count for identical content, with no sentence reaching parity in any tokenizer. This confirms, for a Pakistani language, the global pattern reported by Petrov et al. (2023) and Ahia et al. (2023). Newer tokenizers reduce the premium substantially, from about five to about three, but the reduction has levelled off: Llama 3, Qwen2 and Command-R differ by less than two per cent despite vocabularies ranging from 128,000 to 256,000 tokens. Doubling the vocabulary did not buy Sindhi parity.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Discussion
chunks.text:
Doubling the vocabulary did not buy Sindhi parity.

RQ2 asked whether Sindhi-specific letters drive fragmentation. They do. The Orthographic Penalty Index reached its maximum of 100 in three of five tokenizers: every occurrence of the 18 Sindhi-specific letters was fragmented, while shared letters were not. This is the study's central empirical contribution. It shows that Sindhi's disadvantage is not only a matter of little data, which is the usual explanation (Joshi et al., 2020), but also of the design of vocabularies around the letters of better-resourced neighbours. Urdu suffers its own orthographic penalties, visible in its high fragmentation in GPT-2 and Command-R, but the letters of the Sindhi alphabet are a distinct and measurable target.

RQ3 asked how frequent Sindhi words are segmented. The qualitative analysis shows that the most frequent grammatical words, especially the light verbs and auxiliaries built on ‫ڪ‬ and ‫,ٿ‬ are broken into byte fragments, that Sindhi saves tokens only where its words overlap with Urdu and Arabic, that Urdu-shaped spellings can be cheaper than standard Sindhi ones, and that token boundaries seldom align with Sindhi morphology. These findings extend Rust et al.'s (2021) link between tokenization and model quality by showing which linguistic units are lost.

RQ4 asked about implications. They are discussed in Section 5.4.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Theoretical contributions
chunks.text: The study makes three theoretical contributions. First, it moves tokenization-equity research from the level of languages to the level of scripts within languages. By separating Sindhi-specific letters from shared ones, the OPI shows that two languages written in the "same" script can be treated very differently, and that the difference is located in identifiable characters. Second, the SATEF framework links orthographic encoding to economic cost and representational quality in a single cascade, providing a vocabulary for discussing AI equity that is precise enough for engineers and accessible enough for policy-makers. Third, the finding that the tokenizer rewards Urdu-shaped spellings connects computational linguistics with sociolinguistics: the prestige hierarchy that Rahman (1996Rahman ( , 2002) ) and Mansoor (2005) describe in Pakistani institutions reappears inside algorithms, where it can quietly shape how people write.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Practical implications for Pakistan
chunks.text:
The findings suggest five practical responses.

Tokenizer audits for Pakistani languages. Institutions that adopt AI for public services, education or media in Sindh should report the token premium and OPI of the systems they use, in the same way that accessibility standards are reported for websites (Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, 2018).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Vocabulary extension.
chunks.text:
Developers of open models used in Pakistan can add the Sindhispecific letters and frequent Sindhi letter sequences to tokenizer vocabularies, a technique shown to benefit low-resource languages (Liang et al., 2023). Qwen2 demonstrates that including the letters removes most byte fragmentation.

3. A Unicode normalisation standard for digital Sindhi. Language authorities, publishers and keyboard developers should agree on normalisation rules for heh, yeh and related letters, so that the same word is encoded the same way (Ali et al., 2019;Unicode Consortium, 2023).

4. Sindhi text data. Because merges are learned from data, open, high-quality Sindhi corpora from newspapers, textbooks and literature are needed so that future tokenizers learn Sindhi words, not only Sindhi letters (Jamro, 2017;Motlani, 2016).

5. Critical AI literacy in English and linguistics education. Teachers and students of English and linguistics in Pakistan should understand that AI systems are not language-neutral. The same prompt costs more and fits less in Sindhi, and this knowledge belongs in curricula on language, technology and power (Bender et al., 2021).

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Limitations
chunks.text: The study has several limitations. First, tokenizers were reconstructed from published vocabularies and merge rules; although control phrases reproduced the reference token identifiers, small differences in pre-tokenization may remain, particularly for Command-R. Second, FLORES-200 consists of translated Wikipedia-style text, which may differ from spontaneous Sindhi on social media or in speech (Goyal et al., 2022). Third, only five tokenizers were analysed, and commercial systems whose tokenizers are not public could not be included. Fourth, the study measured tokenization, not downstream model quality; the representational layer of SATEF is inferred from prior research rather than tested. Fifth, the morph-aligned code relies on a rule-based list of endings and would benefit from expert morphological annotation. Finally, the analysis covers Sindhi in the Perso-Arabic script used in Pakistan, not Sindhi in Devanagari as used in India.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Conclusion
chunks.text:
This study asked what it costs, in the currency of AI, to speak Sindhi rather than English. The answer is precise: about 2.9 to 5.0 times as many tokens for the same content, between one quarter and two fifths of the context window, and a systematic penalty on the very letters that make Sindhi Sindhi.

In three of the five tokenizers analysed, every occurrence of the 18 Sindhi-specific letters was broken into byte fragments, while letters shared with Arabic and Urdu were kept whole. Qualitatively, the commonest grammatical words of Sindhi are built from meaningless pieces, its morphology is rarely visible in token boundaries, and Urdu-shaped spellings are rewarded.

The paper's new ideas are the concept of the Sindhi token tax, the Orthographic Penalty Index, and the Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework. Together they show that tokenization inequity is not only a consequence of limited data but also a matter of design at the level of the script, and that it can be measured, audited and corrected. The case of Qwen2 shows that change is possible: including Sindhi letters in the vocabulary removes most fragmentation, although parity will require Sindhi text data as well.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Conclusion
chunks.text:
The case of Qwen2 shows that change is possible: including Sindhi letters in the vocabulary removes most fragmentation, although parity will require Sindhi text data as well.

For Pakistan, where English holds institutional prestige and Sindhi carries the lives of millions, the lesson is that the old hierarchy of languages is being rebuilt inside new technologies. Linguists, educators, developers and policy-makers can prevent this by treating tokenization as a languagepolicy question. Future research should measure downstream model quality alongside tokenization, extend the OPI to Punjabi (Shahmukhi), Pashto, Balochi and Saraiki, and test vocabulary-extension methods designed specifically for Pakistani scripts.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Figure 1
chunks.text: Figure 1: Figure 1.The Script-Aware Tokenization Equity Framework (SATEF) Layer 1, Orthographic equity, asks whether the letters of a language's alphabet are represented as whole units in the tokenizer's vocabulary, whether they are split into bytes, and whether the language's digital text uses Unicode consistently (Unicode Consortium, 2023; Xue et al., 2022).It is measured here by the Orthographic Penalty Index.

Distribution of the sentence-level token premium for Sindhi and Urdu relative to English Quantitative interpretation of Figure 3.The median Sindhi premium was 4.98 for GPT-2, 4.23 for Llama 2, 2.86 for Llama 3, 2.86 for Qwen2 and 2.85 for Command-R.No single sentence in any tokenizer reached parity with English; even the lower whiskers stay well above the dashed parity

chunks.text: Figure 5: Figure 5. Percentage of characters split across tokens in running textQuantitative interpretation of Figure5.English characters were essentially never split (at most 0.03%).For Sindhi, 37.2% of characters were split into byte fragments by GPT-2, around 12% by Llama 2, Llama 3 and Command-R, and 3.9% by Qwen2.Urdu fragmentation followed a different profile: very high in GPT-2 (56.4%), moderate in Llama 3 (14.4%)and Command-R (16.5%), and almost zero in Qwen2 (0.1%).Chi-square tests showed that Sindhi and Urdu fragmentation differed significantly in every tokenizer (χ² from 145.9 to 7,277.2, all p < .001).Sindhi fragmented more than Urdu in Llama 2 and Qwen2, and less in the others.Qualitative reading of Figure5.The Qwen2 result is the key to interpreting this figure.Qwen2 represents almost every Urdu character whole, yet still fragments 3.9% of Sindhi characters.The

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Figure 8
chunks.text: Figure 8: Figure 8. Sindhi token premium (Llama 3) by topic domain Quantitative interpretation of Figure 8.The Sindhi premium differed significantly across the seven topic domains, Kruskal-Wallis H = 77.24,p < .001(Llama 3); the same test on Command-R gave H = 79.11,p < .001.Median premiums ranged from 3.04 for travel and 2.98 for science and technology down to 2.65 for sports and 2.71 for geography.Qualitative reading of Figure 8. Travel and science sentences contain many foreign names and technical terms.In English these are compact, often single tokens; in Sindhi they are transliterated into Perso-Arabic script letter by letter and are rarely present in the tokenizer's merges.The domains in which Pakistan most needs AI support, including science education and health, are therefore among the more expensive for Sindhi users.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Figure
chunks.text: Figure 10.Segmentation typology of the 80 most frequent Sindhi words across tokenizers Quantitative interpretation of Figure 10 (coding output).Of the 80 most frequent Sindhi words, GPT-2 fragmented 73 into bytes and kept none whole.Llama 2 kept none whole, segmented 48 character by character and byte-fragmented 31.Llama 3 and Command-R kept 21 and 22 words whole, respectively, but still byte-fragmented 35 each.Qwen2 kept 8 whole, byte-fragmented only 10, and segmented most of the rest into single characters (27) or arbitrary pieces (29).For comparison, every one of the 80 most frequent English words was a single token in all five tokenizers.The mean number of tokens per frequent Sindhi word was 4.80 (GPT-2), 3.70 (Llama 2), 2.82 (Llama 3), 2.80 (Qwen2) and 2.84 (Command-R), against exactly 1.00 for English.

chunks.header: THE SINDHI TOKEN TAX: ORTHOGRAPHIC PENALTY AND TOKENIZATION INEQUITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND SINDHI IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS > Figure 11
chunks.text: Figure 11: Figure 11.A single Sindhi sentence segmented by five tokenizers, with its English equivalent Quantitative interpretation of Figure 11.The sentence (FLORES id 5) reads, in English, 28-year-old Vidal had joined Barça three seasons ago, from Sevilla.English needed 16 to 21 tokens.Sindhi needed 61 tokens in GPT-2, 64 in Llama 2, 34 in Llama 3 and 36 in Qwen2 and Command-R.Qualitative reading of Figure 11.The red blocks mark byte fragments, and in the 2024 tokenizers they fall exactly on the most Sindhi parts of the sentence.In Llama 3 and Command-R, all five fragmented characters are distinctively Sindhi: ‫ڊ‬ in the name ‫وڊال‬ (Vidal), ‫ٽ‬ in ‫ي‬ ‫ٽ‬ (three), ‫ڪ‬ in ‫ا‬ ‫اراڪ‬ ‫ب‬ (Barça), ‫ٿ‬ in ‫يو‬ ‫ٿ‬ (became), and ‫۾‬ (U+06FE), the special Sindhi sign for the postposition in.Qwen2 fragments only ‫.ٽ‬In GPT-2, by contrast, fragmentation spreads to shared letters as well (14 characters).The proper nouns, spelled with shared letters, are split into short sequences of whole letters, while the Sindhi grammatical words are broken below the level of the letter.The figure makes visible what the statistics describe: the cost falls on what is most Sindhi in the sentence.
